terrain.difficultyNotes: A three-tier breakdown with the top tier the largest at 38%, which sounds impressive until you put it against the mountain: 24 trails on 100 acres with 1,016 feet of vertical. Thirty-eight percent of 24 trails is nine runs, and a black at a southern New Hampshire hill this size is not a black at Cannon. Everything in this group comes from OnTheSnow rather than the resort: crotchedmtn.com is a Vail property and its mountain information page was returning a system-outage error on the verified date. The number that actually defines this mountain is the 63 inches of natural snow, the lowest on this roster, set against 100 acres of snowmaking - which is to say all of it. Crotched is a fully manufactured ski area, and it is very good at being one.

The season pass figure is the full adult (31+) Epic Pass; Vail does not sell an unrestricted Crotched-only pass. Crotched carries unlimited access on the Epic Local Pass too, at $829 for 31+, and for a mountain this size that cheaper tier is the only one that makes sense. crotchedmtn.com was returning a system-outage error on the verified date, so the figures come from OnTheSnow's Epic buyer's guide; that guide quotes $1,089 in its prose, which was the March 2026 on-sale price, while its current cost line reads $1,119.

editorial.overview: Crotched is the smallest mountain in this guide and it has built a genuine identity out of the one thing it can do that bigger mountains cannot be bothered to: it stays open at night, on all of it. A hundred acres, 24 trails, 1,016 feet of vertical in Bennington, an hour from Boston and forty minutes from Manchester, with night skiing Tuesday through Saturday until 9pm and the Midnight Madness sessions running 8pm to midnight on selected dates through the winter. Nobody in New England lights this proportion of their mountain and nobody else keeps a lift spinning past eleven. That is what Crotched is for, and it fills the hill with a young Boston-and-Manchester crowd on weeknights that gives the place an atmosphere the daytime skiing does not earn on its own. Because with 63 inches of natural snow a year - the lowest total on this roster - everything you ski here is made, and 100 acres is a small canvas. Come for a Wednesday night. Do not plan a February Saturday around it.
editorial.snowQuality: Sixty-three inches is the lowest natural snowfall of any resort in this guide and the number is not close - it is half of what Gunstock gets an hour north and a third of Wildcat's. Southern New Hampshire at 2,000 feet simply does not get much snow, and Crotched's answer is complete: 100 acres of snowmaking against 100 skiable acres, so every trail on the mountain is machine-covered. The system is good and the mountain is reliably open, which for a hill this far south is the whole achievement. What it means for a skier is that the surface is manufactured all season and the freeze-thaw cycles of southern New Hampshire are the thing to watch - a January thaw here is a real event in a way it is not at Sugarloaf.
editorial.crowds: Two different mountains depending on the hour. Daytime weekends draw a Boston and Manchester day-trip crowd onto 100 acres and five lifts, which is not much terrain to spread people over, and it feels full. The night sessions are the interesting half: a younger, more local crowd, more of it in the terrain park than on the trails, and a genuinely good atmosphere on a Tuesday or Wednesday evening. Midnight Madness nights sell the place out in a different way - it becomes an event rather than a ski day, which is either the appeal or the problem depending on what you came for.
editorial.difficulty: Small, and the percentages flatter it. Thirty-eight percent of the trails carry the top rating, but 38% of 24 trails is nine runs on 1,016 feet of vertical, and the pitch that earns a black diamond at a southern New Hampshire hill would be a blue at Cannon. There is glade skiing, but on 63 inches of natural snow it opens rarely. What Crotched is honestly good for is a competent skier who wants laps rather than a challenge - five lifts on 100 acres means very short rides and a lot of runs in an evening - and for park riders, who get most of the mountain's attention. Nobody should drive past Gunstock to ski Crotched's terrain in daylight.

keyTrails.name: The night terrain
keyTrails.note: OnTheSnow records 100 acres lit against 100 acres skiable - the entire mountain stays open after dark, which no other resort in this guide can say.

keyTrails.name: Midnight Madness
keyTrails.note: Not a trail but the reason people come: skiing and riding from 8pm to midnight on selected dates through the winter. There is nothing else like it in New England.

moguls.policy: A mountain covering 100 of its 100 acres with snowmaking is protecting a manufactured surface, and that means comprehensive grooming - a hundred acres of machine snow left to bump up would be unskiable within a week at southern New Hampshire temperatures. No grooming policy is published and the resort's site was unreachable, so this is inference from the snowmaking figure rather than a sourced statement, and it is recorded at the cautious end.
moguls.quality: There is no meaningful bump skiing at Crotched and nothing here pretends otherwise. This is a 100-acre fully manufactured mountain whose freestyle attention goes into its parks and whose distinguishing feature is that the lights stay on. Anyone in southern New Hampshire who wants moguls is looking at Gunstock's Tiger terrain an hour north, or Wildcat if they are willing to drive.

parks.overview: Undocumented. crotchedmtn.com was returning a system-outage error on the verified date, OnTheSnow publishes no park count, and there is no independent review of the mountain to fall back on. Crotched has a well-known park scene among southern New Hampshire riders and the Dew After Dark branding on its late-night sessions points squarely at it, but none of that is a source for a count or a name.
parks.reputation: Widely understood locally to be a park-and-night mountain rather than a skier's mountain, and the evening programming is built around that crowd. Nothing citable was found to describe the parks themselves, so no judgement is recorded. Along with Attitash, this is the thinnest parks section on the roster and both should be redone once Vail's site is readable.
